problem: "A pump would cavitate on a mixture; a compressor can handle it" says a compressor can tolerate a two-phase mixture. That is wrong: liquid droplets entering a compressor cause slugging and valve damage, which is exactly why superheat is used (as the chapter itself says in Section 2). The sentence also contradicts the line just before it, that the compressor handles vapour, not a mixture.
fix: "A pump cavitates on a vapour-liquid mixture, so the loop is built so that the compressor takes dry vapour. Liquid carried over into the compressor damages it, which is why a little suction superheat is always provided."

problem: "Condensation 2→3 lies inside the dome" is not true as stated. Compression 1→2 starts at saturated vapour and, being isentropic, ends superheated, so state 2 sits outside the dome; only the later part of 2→3 (the condensation itself) is the horizontal line inside the dome.
fix: "After isentropic compression, state 2 lies in the superheated region, so 2→3 first desuperheats outside the dome and then condenses as a horizontal line inside the dome at condenser temperature."

problem: "read from enthalpy values, not from steam tables alone" suggests steam tables are partly used for a refrigerant. Refrigerant properties come from refrigerant tables or charts, not steam tables.
fix: "Its performance is read from refrigerant property tables or a p-h chart, because the expansion valve is isenthalpic and every term in the COP is an enthalpy difference."

problem: "Using h3 − h4 as work" is a confusing trap as written, because h3 = h4, so the quantity is simply zero. The mistake actually worth warning about is taking the condenser heat h2 − h3 as the work input.
fix: "Using the condenser heat h2 − h3 as work input. The only work input is the compressor work h2 − h1; the throttle gives no shaft work at all."
